tier_reason: README Benchmark section shows first-party do-you-even-bench output (bench.js is public) with wasmrandom 81,321,598.18 op/s vs Math.random 73,658,101.35 op/s vs seedrandom 24,057,933.98 op/s and a uniform frequency check, Node v10.3.0 stated, but no CPU model and an unpinned AssemblyScript master build, so C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: README numbers were measured on the August 2018 build: asc --baseDir assembly -Oz -b index.wasm -t index.wat index.ts --sourceMap --noDebug (package.json at commits c7cf3b3 and e5e290b), with AssemblyScript from GitHub master, unpinned. The current -O3 --validate build and the 52-bit next() float conversion came in commit bc56b66 (2019-01-02) and were never re-benchmarked. Run with Node.js v10.3.0, node --expose-gc bench.js (do-you-even-bench).
corrections.caveats: Node 10.3 era numbers (V8 6.7), no CPU stated; the margin over Math.random is only about 10% (derived from page data), and the seeded JS competitor is seedrandom's default ARC4 generator (a slower algorithm). The README numbers predate the 2019-01-02 commit that switched the build from -Oz to -O3 and changed next() from a 53-bit multiply to a 52-bit mantissa trick; that commit fixed no correctness bug (the 2018 xoroshiro128** update is equivalent to the reference), but the published numbers are for the older build. Each call crosses the JS-to-WASM boundary; there is no batch API. Abandoned since 2019.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly and the benchmark is real (bench.js increments a frequency array and prints uniform counts, so not a no-op). Main shortcomings: no CPU model, only about 1.10x over V8 Math.random on Node 10.3, and the numbers were taken on the 2018 -Oz build rather than the current -O3 one. License BSD-2-Clause (LICENSE.md), 13 stars, last commit 2019-01-02, all as recorded.

notes: Kept at D: real production component, but the only evidence is a no-numbers README sentence. Main shortcomings: no measurement at all and a non-OSI source-available license. Metadata checked: 212 stars, last commit 2022-12-01 (abandoned), not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: benches/results holds first-party criterion runs on named CPUs against the library's own scalar loop, and the bench code that produced them is public (benches/bench_<type>.rs at v0.4.0, commit 74436c9). But the rustc version is not stated anywhere for those rows: no rust-toolchain.toml existed then, and the nightly-2026-10-06 pin is today's HEAD. The rows date from 2023-02-03 and predate later fixes to the float paths (#40 scalar ignore-NaN double update, #100 f16 -0.0/0.0, #102 NaN-ignore with only infinities left), so C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: The rows in benches/results were measured at v0.4.0 (file last changed 2023-02-03, commit 74436c9) with an unstated rustc version; no rust-toolchain.toml existed then, and HEAD now pins nightly-2026-10-06. Built with cargo bench using criterion 0.3 and codspeed-criterion-compat, the default bench profile and no RUSTFLAGS or target-cpu (kernels picked by runtime feature detection). The code is benches/bench_<type>.rs at that commit (row names scalar_random_long_*); the current benches emit scalar_<type>_argminmax rows instead, so HEAD's bench code no longer reproduces these row names.
corrections.workload: Single-pass argmin and argmax over a 102,400-element uniformly random array (ARRAY_LENGTH_LONG in dev_utils/src/config.rs, the same at v0.4.0 and HEAD) for i8..u64, f16, f32 and f64. Runtime-dispatched SSE, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512 or NEON kernels (the impl_* rows) are timed against the library's own scalar loop (the scalar_* rows).
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Benchmarks on my laptop (AMD Ryzen 7 4800U, 1.8 GHz, 16GB RAM) using criterion show that the function is 3-20x faster than the scalar implementation (depending of data type)'. benches/results rows (v0.4.0, 2023), Ryzen 7 4800U: i16 scalar 74.039 us vs impl 4.4617 us (about 16.6x, derived from page data); i8 scalar 76.858 us vs impl 7.2931 us (about 10.5x, derived); f32 scalar 65.058 us vs impl 11.186 us (about 5.8x, derived); f16 scalar 97.594 us vs impl 4.6024 us (about 21.2x, derived). Low end on the same CPU: f64 66.831 us vs 22.857 us (about 2.9x, derived) and u64 74.233 us vs 31.163 us (about 2.4x, derived), so the README's 3x lower bound is slightly overstated. i7-1185G7: f32 scalar 55.549 us vs impl 6.9749 us (about 8.0x, derived).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 64 stars; 15,387,918 crates.io downloads (2,967,157 recent); reverse dependencies include polars-ops and polars-utils; implements traits for ndarray and Arrow arrays
corrections.caveats: The baseline is the library's own scalar loop, not a third-party implementation (NumPy, std iterator min_by_key). The results file is stale: last changed 2023-02-03 at v0.4.0, while the crate is now 0.7.0 with later perf work (#88, #104) and correctness fixes on the float paths (#40 scalar ignore-NaN double update in March 2023, #100 f16 -0.0/0.0 equality and #102 NaN-ignore with only infinities left in October 2026). The toolchain for the rows is unstated. Some x86 SIMD kernels are slower than scalar (Xeon E5-2650 v2: SSE i64 140.98 us vs scalar 98.203 us; SSE u64 157.79 us vs 124.12 us), so dispatch falls back to scalar there. AVX-512 is slower than SSE for i8 and u8 on the i7-1185G7 (10.491 us vs 6.7829 us for i8). On the Raspberry Pi 3B and 4B the f64, i64 and u64 rows had no SIMD path at v0.4 (impl equals scalar). Several rows are annotated slower than v0.3, and the author's own remark says v0.4 is a lot slower on ARM than v0.3.1.

notes: All quoted numbers match benches/results, but those rows are first-party, about 3.7 years old (v0.4.0) and from an unstated rustc version, so not A; down to C. Main shortcomings: stale results versus the current 0.7.0 code (float paths fixed since), self-baseline scalar loop, the README 3-20x range understates the 2.4x u64 low end, and SSE i64/u64 is slower than scalar on the Xeon E5-2650 v2. Notable as a Polars dependency (15.4M crates.io downloads).
